source.version_note: International Journal of Selection and Assessment 34(1):e70039, issue February 2026; Crossref first online 26 December 2025. Supplied copyright 2025 and 2026 issue year are compatible. Interviews collected early 2020.
source.verification_method: All fifteen pages read including interview scenario in Appendix A, coding method, theme counts, limitations and references. Crossref verifies article dates, original reused-study identity and selected reference corrections.

citation.title: “It Feels Wrong”: Understanding Reactions to Artificial Intelligence as a Decision-Maker in Selection Through the Lens of Moral Foundations Theory
citation.venue: International Journal of Selection and Assessment 34(1):e70039

reading.source_scope_note: Qualitative reanalysis of 33 early 2020 interviews about a hypothetical asynchronous AI-evaluated job interview. Moral-foundation coding organizes expressed expectations, not observed discrimination, measured real AI capacities or a demonstrated causal intuition-to-rationalization sequence. The reused dataset is not a new replication of the 2021/2022 original study.
access_limits: All fifteen supplied pages and Appendix A read. Raw transcripts are not shared due to privacy/ethical restrictions; no request or external contact was made.

Crossref checks concern identity/version metadata only. Full original Mirowska/Mesnet, Newman/Fast/Harmon, Haidt books and other primary cognitive studies remain unread and are not counted as additional completed papers.

study.data_reuse: Reanalyzes interviews collected for Mirowska/Mesnet's Preferring the devil you know, first online 2021, print 2022. The new MFT coding is a distinct article/analysis but uses the same respondents, not an independent sample.
study.sample: 33 adults living in France, recruited from the first author's networks, early 2020.18 men/15 women; age 20–59, 17 aged 30–39.25 full-time, 3 part-time, 5 not working.12 French/21 English interviews by a bilingual research assistant, mean 59 minutes, range 40–91.
study.scenario: CV accepted, receive a link, record answers at home, machine-learning evaluation, no direct recruiter contact and algorithm-based feedback. No actual AI interview is conducted; AI evaluation is bundled with asynchronous recording and absent interpersonal exchange.
study.prompts: General AI familiarity plus expected preparation, questions, feedback, human comparison, likes/dislikes, performance and organization impressions. No explicit moral-foundation definitions are supplied, but the guide specifically asks about disabled candidates, as endnote 1 discloses.
study.coding: Six preselected MFT parent categories, inductive subthemes. First author recodes all transcripts; second reviews coding and uncoded passages.11 disputed references resolved in two nonanonymous two-coder consensus rounds described as adapted Delphi. Consensus is not independent inter-rater reliability or proof of unbiased classification.
study.themes: Aggregate coded mentions: fairness 169, sanctity 77, liberty 71, care 68, authority 32, loyalty 13. These exceedN 33 and represent references, not independent people, percentages endorsing a theory or six foundations present in every respondent.
study.findings: Participants anticipate lost dialogue/feedback, reduction of hard-to-quantify qualities, power/oversight concerns, data intrusion and pressure to conform. Some also anticipate fairer standardized treatment, accessibility and richer feedback. None of those expectations is a measured AI outcome.
study.mechanism_scope: Immediate discomfort and later reasons are interpreted through intuitive primacy and post-hoc rationalization. Interview quotations do not establish precise cognitive timing, irrationality or that reasons were not valid prior concerns.

summary: Add intuitive primacy, post-hoc rationalization and perceived algorithmic reductionism as distinct concepts, with theoretical-versus-qualitative scope. Enrich existing reciprocity, conformity, algorithm-aversion and dumbfounding boundaries without treating all moral concerns as fear or all six coding foundations as proven mechanisms.

findings.definition: The view that an intuitive judgment can arise before conscious reasoning about it.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Explicit secondary theoretical principle; interview reactions illustrate compatibility but do not experimentally establish process order or an AI analogue
findings.ai_proposal: Study whether an evaluator commits to an initial verdict before weighing relevant evidence, then tests or merely supports that verdict. For AI, use controlled prompt/order comparisons and observable records without claiming that a language model has a gut feeling or that generated reasoning reveals its full internal computation.
findings.novelty_rationale: A claim about temporal priority of intuition differs from emotion-as-evidence, a conflict between two processes, or generating later justifications. Intuition may be followed by genuine reconsideration rather than rationalization, as the source itself allows.

evidence.quote: One of the key principles of MFT is intuitive primacy
intuitions come first and conscious reasoning follows

findings.evidence_scope: Theoretical background explicitly defines intuitive primacy and discusses gut reactions. Participants describe discomfort and uncertainty about explaining it; no reaction-time manipulation, process tracing or randomized reasoning intervention identifies intuition as the initial cause. The original Haidt works remain secondary references here.
findings.boundary: An immediate response can reflect valid expertise or legitimate concern. Later reasons need not be false or fabricated, and deliberation can change a judgment. Neither interview discomfort nor an AI's first answer proves an automatic emotional mechanism or conscious intuition.

findings.definition: Constructing reasons after a judgment or reaction to justify it, rather than those reasons necessarily having produced it.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Explicitly discussed theoretical interpretation, not an independently identified cause of these interview explanations or proof of unfaithful model reasoning
findings.ai_proposal: Check whether an AI's explanation of a prior action is supported by available records or merely a plausible retrospective story. Distinguish verified sequence, inference and unknown cause; use counterfactual evidence tests rather than accepting an eloquent self-explanation as an execution trace.
findings.novelty_rationale: Retrospective justification is narrower than all motivated reasoning and differs from a group's collective dismissal of warnings. It also differs from any explanation written later: the question is whether the offered reasons actually account for the judgment.

evidence.quote: intuitive response, followed by post hoc rationalizing
the post hoc rationalization that takes

findings.evidence_scope: The authors frame discomfort followed by articulated concerns as compatible with a social-intuitionist account. No independent cognitive record distinguishes rationalization from accurate elaboration or reconsideration. This is a conceptual source, not a causal demonstration or a clinical diagnosis.
findings.boundary: A later explanation can be true, reasoned and useful. Rationalization need not involve conscious deception, and uncertainty about a cause does not justify inventing one. Human retrospective justification and model rationale unfaithfulness are related evaluation concerns, not established identical internal processes.

findings.definition: Perceiving algorithmic evaluation as overlooking important human qualities or context by reducing people to limited measurable features.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Named secondary construct illustrated by qualitative applicant expectations; actual model features, predictive validity and unfairness are not audited
findings.ai_proposal: Compare an AI evaluation's documented feature set with relevant qualitative context and legitimate decision criteria, and separately measure whether affected people perceive reductionism. Provide avenues for context and challenge without assuming unstructured human intuition is automatically fairer or more accurate.
findings.novelty_rationale: A particular perception of algorithmic judgment differs from actually ignoring all unmeasurable factors, treating people solely as means or simply disliking algorithms. The discussion explicitly connects impersonal treatment and hard-to-quantify qualities with the named reductionism literature.
findings.evidence_scope: Participants anticipate loss of contextual judgment, unusual profiles, potential and interpersonal understanding. The authors link those concerns to Newman/Fast/Harmon 2020. No actual interview algorithm is examined; perceived omissions may be correct, mistaken or partly due to asynchronous rather than AI evaluation.
findings.boundary: All evaluations simplify information; structured relevant criteria can improve fairness. The concern requires attention to what matters for the decision, not an assumption that every unquantified intuition deserves weight. A perception does not prove actual discrimination, dehumanization or inferior predictive performance.

findings.term: Applicants expect a reciprocal exchange for interview effort
findings.definition: Applicants expect information, cues, explanations or feedback in return for the time and effort of answering selection questions.
findings.novelty_rationale: A concrete anticipated reciprocity expectation, distinct from felt mutual emotion or an obligation to agree with an evaluator.

evidence.quote: in exchange for the stress and time invested in a job

findings.evidence_scope: Interviewees describe expected dialogue, real-time cues and post-performance feedback. These are expressed expectations in a hypothetical one-way interview, not an experimentally measured reciprocity-induced behavior or proof every automated format lacks such returns.
findings.boundary: Information exchange, emotional reciprocity and benefit repayment differ. An organization's duties require independent ethical/contractual grounds, not any expectation whatever. Fair feedback need not require pretending a model has feelings or creating unnecessary interpersonal attachment.

findings.term: Anticipated conformity to an algorithm's presumed expectations
findings.definition: Applicants say they would alter wording, humor or nonverbal behavior to match what they think an AI evaluator expects.
findings.novelty_rationale: A contextual self-reported conformity intention, not a new algorithmic-conformity syndrome or a direct replication of Asch majority pressure.

evidence.quote: the goal with talking to AI
is to conform, not be an outlier

findings.evidence_scope: Participants anticipate adapting vocabulary, cultural references and expression to presumed evaluation features. No actual interview, scoring model, randomized pressure or observed self-presentation change tests those intentions. Majority agreement is not manipulated.
findings.boundary: Appropriate communication adaptation can be legitimate and need not involve deception or harmful conformity. Presumed algorithm criteria may be wrong. Human candidates' anticipated impression management is not evidence of model sycophancy or the same mechanism as Asch conformity.

findings.term: Discomfort without an immediate explanation does not prove moral dumbfounding
findings.definition: Saying that an AI-led interview feels wrong while initially struggling to explain it does not establish persistent inability to give reasons after challenge.
findings.novelty_rationale: A boundary with the existing dumbfounding phenomenon; later articulated concerns and an untested intuition-first account are not equivalent to a classic dumbfounding task.
findings.evidence_scope: The interview includes uncertainty and discomfort but also numerous substantive concerns. There is no standardized counterargument/challenge procedure or proof those concerns are causally inert. This is not another direct dumbfounding study.
findings.boundary: Lack of a quick explanation can reflect difficulty articulating a valid concern, language choice or uncertainty. It does not prove irrationality, invalid moral perception or an AI's conscious intuition.

findings.term: Algorithm reluctance can coexist with recognition of benefits
findings.definition: People can oppose AI's role in consequential evaluation while acknowledging possible standardization, accessibility or bias-reduction benefits.
findings.novelty_rationale: Contextual qualitative evidence and conditions for an existing preference construct; discomfort need not be blanket fear of all technology.

evidence.quote: despite their stated comfort with advanced
reacting to the AVI structure rather than AI nature

findings.evidence_scope: Interviewees describe mixed views about AI evaluation and human oversight. A single bundled scenario lacks randomized human/AI or synchronous/asynchronous comparators. Benefit expectations are not actual performance data and the reused sample is not an independent replication.
findings.boundary: Reluctance can have legitimate autonomy, accountability, accommodation and privacy grounds. It is not automatically technophobia, ignorance or inaccurate comparison. No evidence here proves a human evaluator is universally superior or an AI is objectively bias-free.

methodological_limits: The study reuses 33 early 2020 interviews from an earlier publication. It is a new interpretive analysis, not 33 new respondents or an independent confirmation of the original sample's reactions.

Convenience/network recruitment in France, small sample, English/French interviews and predominantly educated working-age adults limit transfer. Table 1 includes 5 not currently working, so all 33 are not employed at interview time. No national prevalence estimate follows.

All reactions concern a hypothetical recorded interview. No actual AI evaluation, hiring outcome, discrimination, privacy invasion or applicant performance is observed. Expectations should not be presented as audited capabilities or harms.

The scenario bundles asynchronous self-recording, no direct recruiter, AI scoring and automated feedback. The authors acknowledge participants may be reacting to the asynchronous format rather than the AI itself; no comparison condition separates them.

No explicit moral-foundation primes are given, but prompts ask about advantages/disadvantages, human comparison and job disability implications. Endnote 1 states disabled candidates were specifically prompted, so those accessibility themes are not wholly spontaneous.

The six parent foundations are chosen deductively in advance, then subthemes induced within them. Finding text that can be mapped to all six supports the framework's interpretive applicability, not independent proof of its universality or six underlying causal mechanisms.

The paper critiques earlier work for not measuring individual moral-foundation endorsement but does not administer participant MFQ scores here. Coded concerns cannot establish endorsement strength, genetic influences or causal moderation by a personality-like foundation score.

First-author coding followed by second-author review and consensus is documented transparently, but it is not fully independent blind coding. Calling the adapted two-person nonanonymous deliberation Delphi does not guarantee unbiased or uniquely correct classification.

Foundations can overlap in interpretation: concern about omitted qualities is classified as sanctity rather than fairness because of inferred sacred human judgment. That theoretical choice is not necessarily the participant's explicit belief and requires care in claiming unconscious motives.

Table 2 counts code references, not independent respondents. Fairness 169 does not mean 169 people, 169 independent observations or that every participant endorsed it more strongly. Unequal interview length/topic prompting can affect reference frequencies.

Absence of experienced harm is not absence of a moral issue. Anticipated constraints, inaccessible process, privacy risks and lack of remedy can be legitimate concerns. The design does not establish that participants moralize an otherwise objectively harmless technology.

Discomfort followed by explanations is compatible with intuitive primacy but does not establish cognitive timing or that later reasons are rationalizations. No independent process measure shows those reasons did not inform the initial response.

Tech-comfortable participants can dislike a particular role for AI; this does not prove an irrational fear or that all unease is a binding-foundation response. Actual knowledge, trust calibration and algorithm performance are not tested.
Participants' stated plans to alter vocabulary, humor or expression are intentions. No actual behavior or scoring outcome verifies conformity, faking, gaming or loss of authentic self-presentation.

Expectations that AI can infer hidden traits, emotions or deception from eye movements are participant beliefs, not validated sensing claims. The paper does not establish that these inferences work, are used by a real system or are ethically justified.

Care/fairness are coded with both benefits and concerns; their suggested tempering role is not an experimentally tested mediator or intervention. Better communications cannot be assumed to resolve actual fairness, consent, accessibility or accountability problems.

Authority/loyalty/sanctity labels describe a proposed explanation, not permission to preserve unjust hierarchy, discriminatory traditions or uncritical group loyalty. MFT's six descriptive foundations are distinct from the project's normative principles and categories.

The data predate widespread generative-AI use. The 2026 issue year should not make readers assume current reactions, exposure or technology. Claims about contemporary hiring-tool use need separate current evidence.
The source's broad GDPR human-in-the-loop summary is not an applicability analysis. No legal entitlement or compliance conclusion is inferred from these preferences or that statement.

A participant identifierP 60 appears in the loyalty passage despite a 33-person sample otherwise usingP 01–P 33. It may be a transcription/reference error; do not silently map it to another person without the transcript/key.

Raw transcripts are withheld for privacy/ethical reasons. Coding validation, translation effects, negative cases and precise source attributions cannot be independently reproduced here. Reading cited books' summaries is not reading those books.

cross_paper_learning.finding: Rejecting a robot's explanation or role need not be technophobia-induced reactance. Here, explicit comfort with technology coexists with context-specific objections; fear, autonomy, semantic interpretation and valid concern remain separate.
Emotional reciprocity, interview information exchange and procedural fairness are different. Perceptions of ethical practice do not independently audit privacy, fairness or actual beneficial effects.

Articulated explanations can illuminate trust and values without uniquely identifying the cause of a prior choice. Neither source's post-task narrative should be treated as a complete internal causal trace.

Named theoretical cues and observed human judgments require separate levels of inference. Just as warmth did not explain the babyface result, coding a concern as sanctity or authority does not establish that mechanism.

deferred.reason: The study identifies moral concerns but does not observe an issue changing from nonmoral to moral over time; no separate process definition or causal transition is established here.

Retain as a contextual concern distinct from general technophobia; the brief consciousness/overtaking definition does not justify adding another broad fear subtype without the original multidimensional source.
Qualitative intentions are captured under existing conformity with a boundary from Asch majority pressure, rather than add a context-only duplicate.
A theoretical interpretation within sanctity coding, not an independently measured inviolable-value mechanism or proof such human roles must always be exclusive.
Important background distinctions, but not separately defined or measured processes here. Seek primary constructs rather than inflate every fairness theme into another behavior.

limitations: Three concepts added with temporal/measurement scope. No automatic ethical edges, unverified hiring capability, independence of reused data, irrationality diagnosis or current legal claim inferred.
